entry: English writer and journalist. He created some of literature's best-known fictional characters and is regarded by many as the greatest novelist of the [[Victorian era]]. His literary success began with the 1836 serial publication of *The Pickwick Papers*, and within a few years he was an international literary celebrity known for his humor, satire and observation of character and society. His novels, most published in monthly or weekly instalments, pioneered the serial publication of narrative fiction. *[[A Christmas Carol|A Christmas Carol]]* (1843) remains especially popular, and *[[Great Expectations|Great Expectations]]* and *Oliver Twist* are frequently adapted. *Bleak House* (1853), a satire on the judicial system, helped support a reformist movement that culminated in 1870s legal reform in England. He also campaigned for children's rights and education. The adjective *Dickensian* describes things reminiscent of his writings, such as poor social or working conditions and comically repulsive characters.

French mathematician. He is known for proving the transcendence of the number [[E (mathematical constant)|*e*]]. In 1842 he published a simple proof of [[Niels Henrik Abel]]'s proposition that equations of the fifth degree have no algebraic solution. In papers published in 1858, 1865 and 1866, he showed that roots of the quintic polynomial could be obtained using elliptic integrals. He corresponded with [[Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi]] on Abelian and elliptic functions. With [[Arthur Cayley]] and James Joseph Sylvester he developed the theory of invariants, and within that work he discovered the law of reciprocity. Elected to the French Academy of Sciences in 1848, he became professor of mathematics at the University of Paris in 1869 and remained there until his death.

King of the United Kingdom and 14 other Commonwealth realms since 2022. The eldest son of [[Elizabeth II]], he was created Prince of Wales in 1958 and succeeded his mother in 2022. He founded The Prince's Trust in 1976 and became patron or president of more than 800 other charities and organizations. As manager of the Duchy of Cornwall estates he supported [[Organic farming|organic farming]] and action on [[Climate change|climate change]], and he has been a prominent critic of genetically modified food. He has drawn scrutiny for his support of [[Alternative medicine|alternative medicine]].

King of England, Scotland, and Ireland (r. 1660–85). The oldest surviving child of [[Charles I of England|Charles I]], he was king of Scotland from 1649 to 1651 and then spent nine years in exile after the [[English Civil War]]. He dissolved Parliament in 1681 and ruled alone until his death. His 1672 Royal Declaration of Indulgence, which sought religious freedom for Catholics and Protestant dissenters, was withdrawn under pressure from Parliament. A patron of the arts and sciences, he had no surviving children with his wife, Catherine of Braganza, but acknowledged at least 12 illegitimate children by various mistresses.

King of Spain (r. 1665–1700). The last member of the [[House of Habsburg]] to rule Spain, he experienced lengthy periods of ill health, which made the question of his succession central to European diplomacy. His death without children led to the [[War of the Spanish Succession|War of the Spanish Succession]] (1701–14). Shortly before dying in November 1700, he named Philip of Anjou, grandson of [[Louis XIV]] of France, as his heir. Either leading candidate acquiring an undivided Spanish Empire threatened the European balance of power, and war followed.

Holy Roman Emperor (r. 1355–78). Born Wenceslaus in [[Prague]], he was the eldest son of John of Bohemia and inherited the County of Luxembourg from his father. He was elected King of the Romans in 1346 and became King of [[Bohemia]] that year. He was crowned King of Italy and Holy Roman Emperor in 1355 and, after his coronation as King of Burgundy at Arles in 1365, became the crowned ruler of all the kingdoms of the [[Holy Roman Empire]]. He founded Charles University in 1348 and made Prague a major European cultural and political hub. The Golden Bull of 1356 marked a structural change in imperial politics. Several aspects of his legacy remain contentious. The image of him as a wise, pious, peace-loving king, partly constructed by Charles himself, has proved influential.

King of England, Scotland, and Ireland (r. 1625–49). He believed in the divine right of kings and quarrelled with Parliament over taxation levied without its consent. His religious policies and his marriage to a Catholic, Henrietta Maria of France, generated mistrust from [[Puritans]] and Scottish Covenanters. His attempt to force the Church of Scotland to adopt high Anglican practices led to the Bishops' Wars, which strengthened the English and Scottish parliaments. From 1642 he fought Parliament's armies in the [[English Civil War]]. After his defeat in 1645 he surrendered to a Scottish force. He refused demands for a [[Constitutional monarchy|constitutional monarchy]] and was tried, convicted and executed for high treason. The monarchy was abolished and a republic established until its restoration in 1660 under his son Charles II.

[[Hong Kong]] electrical engineer. Born in Shanghai, he studied electrical engineering in London. In 1966, while working at Standard Telecommunication Laboratories in Harlow, England, he laid the groundwork for [[Optical fiber|fiber optics]] in communication. In the 1960s he had devised methods to combine glass fibers with [[Laser|lasers]] to transmit digital data, which laid the groundwork for the evolution of the [[Internet]] and the [[World Wide Web]]. In 2009 he shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Willard S. Boyle and George E. Smith for work on the transmission of light in fibers for optical communication. He was knighted in 2010. He was a permanent resident of Hong Kong and a citizen of the United Kingdom and the United States.

English actor and director. He won the Academy Award for Best Actor for his portrayal of [[Henry VIII]] in *The Private Life of Henry VIII* (1933). Born in the North Riding of [[Yorkshire]], he trained at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London. His films include *Mutiny on the Bounty* (1935), *The Hunchback of Notre Dame* (1939) and *[[Spartacus (film)|Spartacus]]* (1960). He directed one film, *The Night of the Hunter* (1955). He earned a motion picture star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 1960.

American aviator, military officer, and author. In 1927 he made the first solo nonstop flight from New York to [[Paris]] in the *Spirit of St. Louis*, covering about 3,600 miles (5,800 km) in over 33 hours. The feat brought him worldwide fame, and [[Time (magazine)|*Time*]] named him its first Man of the Year. In 1932 his infant son was kidnapped and murdered, prompting the U.S. to make [[Kidnapping|kidnapping]] across state lines a federal crime. With French surgeon Alexis Carrel he worked on a perfusion pump, a device credited with making later [[Transplantation (medicine)|organ transplantation]] possible. Before the United States entered [[World War II]], he opposed American intervention. His statements about Jews and race led many to believe he was a Nazi sympathizer, though he never publicly stated support for the Nazis and condemned them several times. He associated with them on numerous occasions in the 1930s and also endorsed eugenic selective breeding. He later became a [[Pulitzer Prize|Pulitzer Prize]]-winning author and helped establish [[National park|national parks]] in the U.S.

Scottish geologist. His *Principles of Geology* (1830–33) presented to a wide audience the idea that the Earth was shaped by natural processes still operating today at similar intensities. The philosopher William Whewell called this gradualistic view "uniformitarianism" and contrasted it with the catastrophism championed by [[Georges Cuvier]]. Building on the work of [[James Hutton]], Lyell favored an indefinitely long age for the Earth. His division of the Tertiary period into the [[Pliocene]], [[Miocene]] and [[Eocene]] was highly influential. His separate period for human history, the "Recent," is widely cited as providing the foundations for the modern discussion of the [[Anthropocene]]. He was a close friend of [[Charles Darwin]] and contributed significantly to Darwin's thinking on the processes of evolution. In 1858 he helped arrange the simultaneous publication of papers by Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace on [[Natural selection|natural selection]], despite his personal religious qualms about the theory.

American cartoonist. He created the comic strip [[Peanuts|*Peanuts*]], which featured Charlie Brown and [[Snoopy]]. United Features Syndicate renamed the strip *Peanuts* when it began publishing in October 1950. Schulz helped write several animated television specials and four animated films based on his characters, beginning with *A Charlie Brown Christmas* in 1965. He drew *Peanuts* until his death. Cartoonists he inspired include [[Matt Groening]], Jim Davis and Bill Watterson.

American criminal and musician. He led the Manson Family, whose followers murdered eight people in the Tate–LaBianca murders in Los Angeles, including actress [[Sharon Tate]] and her unborn child. The murders triggered a wave of fear across the United States. Manson drew on lyrics by [[The Beatles|the Beatles]] to adopt the term "Helter Skelter" for an impending race war. Prosecutors argued that he intended to start a race war, a claim he disputed. He denied ordering any murders and spent the rest of his life in prison.

Frankish military and political leader. Known by the sobriquet "Martel," meaning "the Hammer," he was Duke and Prince of the [[Franks]] and Mayor of the Palace, and de facto ruler of the Franks from 718 until his death. He restored centralized government in [[Francia]] and campaigned until the Franks were the undisputed masters of all of [[Gaul]]. He gained a victory against an invasion of Aquitaine by the [[Umayyad Caliphate]] at the Battle of Tours, which curbed the spread of Islam in [[Western Europe]]. He is also traditionally credited with a role in developing the Frankish system of [[Feudalism|feudalism]]. At the end of his reign he divided Francia between his sons, Carloman and Pepin, and Pepin became the first king of the Carolingian dynasty. Pepin's son [[Charlemagne]] extended the Frankish realms. Older historiography calls Charles illegitimate, but the line between wives and concubines was not clear-cut in 8th-century Francia.

French author. He laid the foundations for the [[Fairy tale|fairy tale]] as a literary genre with *Histoires ou contes du temps passé* (1697). Its best-known tales include "[[Little Red Riding Hood]]," "[[Cinderella]]," "Puss in Boots," "Sleeping Beauty" and "Bluebeard." Some of his versions of older stories influenced the German versions published by the [[Brothers Grimm]] more than 100 years later. A member of the Académie française, he was the leader of the Moderns in the Quarrel of the Ancients and the Moderns. He advised [[Louis XIV]] to place 39 fountains, each representing one of Aesop's fables, in the labyrinth of Versailles.

Iraqi-born British businessman and art collector. He co-founded the advertising agency Saatchi & Saatchi with his brother Maurice in 1970, and the agency became the world's largest in the 1980s. Its work included the [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative Party]]'s 1979 election campaign, led by [[Margaret Thatcher]], with the slogan "Labour Isn't Working." The brothers left the agency in 1995 and formed M&C Saatchi. He owns the Saatchi Gallery and sponsored the Young British Artists, including Damien Hirst and Tracey Emin. Critics have accused him of market manipulation through bulk purchases.

American scientist, mathematician, logician, and philosopher. Sometimes known as "the father of [[Pragmatism|pragmatism]]," he made major contributions to [[Logic|logic]], including theories of relations and quantification. He was a founder of [[Semiotics|semiotics]], the study of signs, and he rigorously formulated [[Mathematical induction|mathematical induction]] and [[Deductive reasoning|deductive reasoning]]. He defined the concept of abductive reasoning and was one of the founders of statistics. As early as 1886 he saw that logical operations could be carried out by electrical switching circuits. Educated as a chemist, he was intermittently employed by the United States Coast Survey between 1859 and 1891, working mainly in [[Geodesy|geodesy]] and gravimetry. Charles William Eliot, president of [[Harvard University|Harvard]], repeatedly vetoed his employment there.

Holy Roman Emperor (r. 1519–56) and King of Spain (r. 1516–56). He was heir to the rising [[House of Habsburg]], and his dominions included the Holy Roman Empire, the Low Countries, the Austrian hereditary lands and Spain with its southern Italian kingdoms. Spanish colonization of the Americas continued under him, and he supported the [[Magellan expedition]], which resulted in the first circumnavigation of the world. He styled himself a new [[Charlemagne]]. He spent most of his life at war with France and the [[Ottoman Empire]], and he declared [[Martin Luther]] an outlaw in 1521. Rome was sacked by his mutinous soldiers in 1527. He abdicated in 1556, dividing his domains between his son [[Philip II of Spain|Philip II]] and his brother Ferdinand, and he retired to the Monastery of Yuste.

King of Sweden (r. 1697–1718). He led Sweden in the [[Great Northern War]] against a coalition of Denmark–Norway, Saxony–Poland–Lithuania and [[Russia]]. His victory over a much larger Russian army at Narva in 1700 compelled [[Peter the Great]] to sue for peace, but Charles rejected the offer. By 1706 he had forced his other foes into submission, and he then marched on Moscow. His army suffered heavy losses at Poltava against a Russian force more than twice its size, and Charles, incapacitated by a wound before the battle, spent years in exile in the [[Ottoman Empire]]. He died during the Siege of Fredriksten in Norway. Sweden lost most of its empire, and its absolute monarchy gave way to a parliamentary government that lasted half a century. He never married.

French general and statesman. He led the Free French Forces against [[Nazi Germany]] and [[Vichy France]] in [[World War II]], and he chaired the Provisional Government of the French Republic from 1944 to 1946. Brought back to power during the 1958 crisis over the [[Algerian War]], he commissioned a new constitution that established the Fifth Republic, and he was elected president later that year. He oversaw Algeria's independence. He withdrew France from [[NATO]]'s integrated military command and built an independent nuclear strike force, making France the world's fourth nuclear power. He restored relations with [[Konrad Adenauer]], and the two signed the Élysée Treaty in 1963. He resigned in 1969 after losing a referendum on decentralization.

Carolingian emperor (r. 881–887). The youngest son of Louis the German and a great-grandson of [[Charlemagne]], he was the last Carolingian emperor of legitimate birth and the last to rule a united kingdom of the [[Franks]]. He inherited all of West Francia in 884, reuniting the [[Carolingian Empire]]. Traditional accounts describe him as lethargic and inept. He was frequently ill, is believed to have had [[Epilepsy|epilepsy]], and twice paid Viking raiders for peace, including at the Siege of Paris. A coup led by his nephew Arnulf of Carinthia deposed him in November 887. The empire then split into five successor kingdoms, and its territory was not reunited under one ruler until the conquests of [[Napoleon]].

Most populous city in South Carolina, on Charleston Harbor. Founded as Charles Town in 1670 and named for [[Charles II of England|Charles II]], it was a primary entry point for the [[Atlantic slave trade]], and almost one-half of enslaved people imported to the United States arrived there. The city formally apologized for its role in the American slave trade in 2018. Its economy is anchored by tourism, port and logistics, aerospace, and information technology, and [[Boeing]] is among its major employers.

Capital and most populous city of West Virginia. Located at the confluence of the Elk and Kanawha rivers, it was formally incorporated in 1794, with [[Daniel Boone]] among its trustees. Salt production drove growth in the 19th century, followed by [[Coal|coal]] mining and [[Natural gas|natural gas]]. The city became the permanent state capital in 1885, and its later economy developed around chemical manufacturing and public-sector employment. The population was 48,864 at the 2020 census.

Terrorist attack in [[Paris]], France, on 7 January 2015. Two French-born Algerian brothers, Saïd and Chérif Kouachi, killed 12 people at the offices of the satirical weekly *Charlie Hebdo*, claiming membership in [[Al-Qaeda|al-Qaeda]] in the Arabian Peninsula. The brothers were killed by the GIGN on 9 January. A related attack on a kosher supermarket killed four people, all Jewish. About 3.7 million people joined demonstrations across France on 11 January, and the next issue of the magazine printed 7.95 million copies. In 2020, 14 accomplices were convicted.

American [[Jazz|jazz]] saxophonist, bandleader, and composer. Known as "Yardbird" or "Bird," he was a highly influential soloist and a leading figure in the development of bebop, a fast, virtuosic style with advanced harmonies. He introduced rapid passing chords, new variants of altered chords and chord substitutions into jazz. He primarily played the alto saxophone. Raised in [[Kansas City, Missouri|Kansas City]], he joined pianist Jay McShann's band in 1938. He later worked with bebop innovators in [[New York City]], including Thelonious Monk and [[Miles Davis]]. He became an icon for the hipster subculture and later the Beat Generation. He received a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 1984.
